entries.title: files and directories with an explicit mode, and exclusive create, in nish:fs
entries.body:
nish:fs gains writeFileSyncMode(path, data, mode), mkdirSyncMode(path, mode)
and createFileExclusiveSync(path, data, mode), so a program can write a
secret at 0600, create a 0700 directory, and take a lock file that exactly
one of several racing processes wins. Each answers the byte count (or 0) or a
negative errno and never exits; a mode outside 0..0o777 answers -22, so the
setuid, setgid and sticky bits are refused.

writeFileSyncMode opens with O_NOFOLLOW and O_CLOEXEC and fchmods the
descriptor to exactly `mode` before the first byte is written, so a file that
already existed at 0644 never holds the new data at 0644 and the umask cannot
widen the result. It truncates and writes in place: a crash leaves the file
empty or partial, and a caller that needs the old file or the new one writes
a temporary with it and renameSyncs it into place. createFileExclusiveSync
opens with O_CREAT|O_EXCL, answers -17 when the path exists (a dangling link
included), and unlinks the file it created if the mode change or the write
then fails, so a failed attempt never leaves a lock behind. mkdirSyncMode
answers -17 for an existing path and leaves its mode alone.

The errno numbers in nish:fs are the platform's, untranslated; the docs show
Linux's and note that Darwin's differ (ELOOP is -62 there). The guide now
says that a native string from String.fromBytes carries any bytes while
--emit-ts decodes UTF-8, so writeBytes and writeFileBytesSync are the route
that is exact on every target.

scripts/fuzz.sh is fixed too. Its sed missed defines with an inline attribute
list, so about thirty JSON codec functions were built without ASan, and its
`grep -q` guard under pipefail let the SIGPIPE it caused read as "no miss".
The sed now appends sanitize_address to any attribute list, and the guard
reads all of grep's output.

The security record adds RT-24 (the mode race on a pre-existing file), RT-25
(symlink following) and RT-26 (umask on mkdir).
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: spawnPiped runs a child with stdin from memory and stdout/stderr captured
entries.body:
nish:process gains spawnPiped(argv, stdin, stdout, stderr), which runs a
child by absolute path or a PATH search, writes `stdin` to it on a pipe, and
appends what it prints to the caller's `stdout` and `stderr` arrays. A secret
can therefore reach `security -i` or `secret-tool store` without touching
argv, the environment or a file. It answers the child's status as spawnSync
encodes it, -1 when the program cannot be started (an empty argv[0], a NUL in
an argument, a missing program), or a distinct negative code when the
captured output passes the byte cap; then the child is killed and reaped.

The result is caller-owned out-params rather than a record, because no
builtin returns a nominal type today; the written arrays must be spelled
`u8[]`, and a typed-array spelling is refused (NL2415) because its length is
fixed. One poll(2) loop drives stdin and both outputs over non-blocking
close-on-exec pipes, so a child that fills its stdout before reading its
stdin cannot deadlock either side. SIGPIPE is blocked around the writes, and
any SIGPIPE the call raised is consumed before the mask is restored. A child
that exits without reading its input does not kill the caller. The runtime
copies nothing out of `stdin`, so there is nothing of the caller's secret
left to wipe. Under Node the call runs child_process.spawnSync with `input`
and a maxBuffer at the same cap, and answers -1 wherever native does.

The escape rule the other spawns have covers spawnPiped's argv, and its out-
params are recorded as written and growable. The security record adds RT-27
to RT-31: deadlock, unbounded output, SIGPIPE, descriptors inherited by the
child (a Darwin window is recorded open), and argv and environment exposure.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: a packing dispatch policy for nish/net/postgres's PgPool
entries.body:
`PgConfig.pack`, false by default, makes `PgPool.dispatch()` hand a request
to the first ready connection with room, filling it to `maxInFlight` before
the next, instead of to the one with the fewest groups in flight. Fewer
connections in use send fuller writes and so fewer packets, which pays on a
lossy link between the program and the server. A connection is still wanted
only once every ready one is full, and a dispatch still costs one pass over
the slots and no allocation. The default is unchanged.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: binary result columns for nish/net/postgres
entries.body: bindStartBinary(name) opens a Bind whose bindEnd() asks for every result column in binary format; binaryInt, binaryBool and binaryFloat on PgConnection and the PgBinary decoders (int, bool, float, timestamp, iso) read int2/int4/int8, bool, float8 and timestamptz in place with no parsing. bindStart/bindEnd and every text path are unchanged. The two extra bytes of a binary bindEnd are kept free under maxOutput, so bindEnd and sync are still never refused for room.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon
